hooks.text: A single sound once traveled across an entire ocean.
How far can the sound of an explosion actually travel?
No sound is supposed to travel across an entire ocean.

title: How Far Did the Sound of Krakatoa's Blast Travel? 😳
description: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa produced the loudest sound in recorded history. This massive volcanic blast was so powerful it was heard thousands of miles away.

beats.text: A single sound once traveled across an entire ocean.
beats.visual: map of the Indian Ocean, engraving, 1880

beats.text: Yet, on August 27, 1883, the volcano Krakatoa erupted.
beats.visual: lithograph of the Krakatoa eruption column, 1888

beats.text: Its forty-meter tsunamis obliterated 165 coastal towns.
beats.visual: engraving depicting tsunami damage along the Sunda Strait coast, 1883

beats.text: The atmospheric shock waves circled the entire globe seven times.
beats.visual: barograph record of the Krakatoa pressure wave, 1888

beats.text: Spectacular crimson skies triggered false fire alarms in New York.
beats.visual: pastel sketch of a crimson sunset over London by William Ascroft, 1883

beats.text: Thousands of kilometers away in central Australia, people heard the rumble.
beats.visual: photograph of Alice Springs in the Australian outback, 19th century

beats.text: Across the Indian Ocean on Rodrigues, they heard the blast.

better_than_last: We updated the hook to a powerful statement rather than a strawman contradiction, and revised the Australian distance reference to strictly adhere to official historical guidelines.
